text.content: 11: Beyond the Ring ust beyond the orbit of Uranus lies humanity’s literal gateway to the galaxy. When the protomolecule arose from the surface of Venus, the “vessel” it constructed moved to this position in the outer Sol system and reassembled itself into a ring-like structure a thousand kilometers across. Since it activated, the Ring has connected the Sol system to a frontier wider, more promising, and far more dangerous than anyone imagined.

The Ring itself is, like most of the Builder technology humans have encountered, simple and utilitarian, lacking all embellishment. Although it’s massive, the Ring appears almost delicate when viewed from a great distance. Up close, it’s vast, and little more than the surface of its event horizon is visible to an approaching ship. Otherwise, the blue glow around the inner edge of the Ring is the only sign that it is active. It emits no signals and somehow maintains a perfect orbital position relative to Sol without thrusters or any other detectable form of propulsion. How the Ring works is a complete mystery; it appears to generate some type of stable wormhole into the space now called the Slow Zone, but the mechanics of such technology is well beyond our grasp. The Ring’s power source may be anything from the distant sun to cosmic background radiation or even something else entirely. Its structure is primarily made of materials “mined” from Eros and Venus, and perhaps the material remains of the more than a million people who were on Eros Station, although people try not to think too much about that. It involves alloys and construction unknown to human science. Scientists are eagerly studying the Ring to learn more about it, but they are proceeding with great care; the last thing they want to do is either disrupt it or cause it to react to a perceived threat, like the hub station did. This makes research slow and difficult since it is largely limited to visual and other surface-level scans. Trying to cut into the surface of the Ring, even to take samples of its material—much less find out what’s inside—has struck everyone as a pretty universally bad idea, no matter how tempting.

Transit

Crossing the event horizon of the Ring leads into, or back out of, the Slow Zone. The same is the case for the other rings in the network. Studying the behavior of the rings and the disappearances of some ships in transit led to the understanding that the rings have some type of limit on the amount of mass they can transit over a given period of time. Exceed that limit and a ship “goes dutchman,” simply disappearing and never reemerging on the other side. Where such ships go and what happens to them remains a mystery, but none have ever returned, and it’s certainly a fate any captain or crew wants to avoid. Since that discovery, which ultimately won the Free Navy Conflict, one of the key roles of the Transport Union has been to monitor gate travel and carefully schedule transits to avoid any other ships “going dutchman.” Thus far, the Union has been quite successful in that regard. It is one of the reasons why the organization limits use of the gate network and takes violations of its planned schedule quite seriously. In addition to posing a potentially deadly hazard for ships by upsetting the transit limits, uncontrolled transits are also a navigational hazard and may cause other potential problems humanity would rather avoid.

Transiting through the Sol gate leads to a space that has become known as “the Slow Zone.”, which came about after the Sol gate triggered some type of defensive mechanism from the hub (see The Hub, following), slowing the passage of all objects through the space. The “speed limit” was lowered during an incident aboard the hub. The limit was later lifted when the hub and the gate network system was “reset”, but the name “Slow Zone” has stuck. The zone is a roughly spherical area about a million kilometers in diameter—the distance from the hub in the center to the rings at the perimeter is about a third more than the average distance from Earth to Luna. Originally, there was nothing in the space apart from the ring station, but its reactivation caused 1,372 other ring gates to appear, spaced evenly around the spherical distance. Medina Station is also now “parked” in the zone, orbiting the hub just beyond the “junk ring”. During the initial exploration of the zone, a considerable amount of debris fell into orbit around the hub, but the station has slowly and methodically cleared most of it. Exactly where the slow zone is remains unclear. The spaces between the rings on the outer perimeter show only a darkly shimmering “non-space” without any visible stars or reference points. Anything passing between, rather than through, the rings and beyond that perimeter simply disappears. Needless to say, this has made studying the phenomenon difficult. In general, most are minded to stay within the bounds of the zone and maintain a proscribed course for one of the rings.

Medina Station

Humanity’s outpost within the slow zone is Medina Station, formerly the OPA battleship Behemoth, formerly the generation ship Nauvoo. Converted from a ship into a station, Medina serves as the waystation and control center for travel through the slow zone and the ring network. Initially held by the OPA and later the Free Navy, Medina is now the key installation of the Transport Union. Ambitious in scale for its time, Medina Station was designed as a generation ship, to function independently across decades, so its structure is still fairly traditional: command center, engineering sections, maintenance and power systems, and the like. It was also designed for people from Earth to make the journey to the stars, although it’s now primarily home to Belters and a small minority of Martians and Earthers. With all of the changes in its mission, Medina Station has more than a few ad hoc adaptations and “make do” refits to meet immediate needs. Since the process of keeping the station up and running requires much of the maintenance crew’s time, most of those modifications fall into the “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” category—at least up until something actually does break. What all of this means is that Medina still keeps some secrets, even decades after settling into the Slow Zone. The main, public areas of the station are well known, but deep inside its hull, much less behind panels and conduits, some things still surprise the people who live and work here: Whole rooms or corridors not exactly where they should be, or assembled differently, or corners cut on the installation of conduits or wiring or the like.

Command

The command center of Medina Station is located in the bow, the end of the drum cylinder opposite the drive section, and situated along its axis. This is so the command decks are always in microgravity unless the station is under thrust, which is basically never except for minor station-keeping in the Slow Zone. This suits the largely Belter crew just fine since they operate without difficulty on the float. A long, curving ramp leads from the drum section into the command area, allowing visitors to acclimate to the change in gravity in either direction. A high-speed lift also runs from one end of the station to the other, allowing for quick transit between the command decks and the engines. Just like on a smaller ship, all of the main systems of Medina Station are controlled from command. This includes helm and navigation (even though the ship is “parked” in its orbit), along with main computer access, environmental controls, and the systems that control the drive and the rotation of the drum. Short of in-person maintenance work, nearly every task the crew needs to do can be handled from the bridge. The command levels still feature some of the touches requested by the original Mormon commissioners of the Nauvoo for their generation ship, including pastoral murals, sunburst and starry night decorations, angelic iconography, stained-glass, and other flourishes that make the area almost cathedral-like. The current crew has gotten used to the look and feel of the place, and there’s an unspoken and somewhat superstitious agreement to leave things as they are, either a reminder of Medina’s history, to honor the events that led to the Union’s formation, or a measure of both.

Defensive Systems

The Behemoth was loaded up for a confrontation, but its glitchy and often hastily-installed weapons have been systematically upgraded and replaced over the years. Medina Station has a substantial enough network of rail guns and torpedo launchers to make it the envy of a UNN or MCRN battleship, along with a full-coverage system of point defense cannons able to take down most incoming weapons. These defensive systems are also controlled from the command decks.

The destroyed rail gun emplacements on the hub station were eventually replaced after the Free Navy Conflict, restoring Medina Station’s control over the slow zone. At least three different rail guns on the hub can target any given ring gate position within the zone, providing a formidable defense.

The Drum

The bulk of Medina Station is taken up by the central drum, a cylinder nearly two kilometers long, which rotates to generate a steady one-sixth g of spin-gravity on its inner surface, light enough for the primarily Belter crew and inhabitants, but heavy enough to allow Martian and Earther visitors to manage without too much difficulty. The drum is capable of spinning up to a full 1 g, but it rarely if ever does. A “sunbeam” of artificially-generated light extends along the axis of the drum, providing the illumination of a clear summer day on Earth, making the spacious inner surface of the drum as close to “outside” space as one can find on a ship or station. It also makes it impossible to look directly across the drum to the other side, making the experience a bit easier for non-Belters. Large parts of the drum’s inner surface area are covered in soil and designated as farmland. It was designed for self-sustaining crop cultivation for the generation ship, and some of “the acres” are still used to grow food crops to supplement the station’s supplies, providing a novel amount of fresh produce out on the edges of human space—something the trades and on-board restaurants use to their advantage. The drum houses the station’s medical facilities, adapted from those originally designed for the generation ship, and its security facilities, placing security personnel closest to the largest concentration of the station’s population. Both coordinate with the command center, but they generally run things without needing to do much more than the occasional check-in and provide regular reports.

The communal and social areas of the inner surface of the drum have been repurposed and converted into what has become known as “the souk,” a colorful bazaar and marketplace for communal activity. It includes various restaurants, cafés, bars, brothels, and nightclubs alongside booths, carts, and shopfronts for local businesses, catering to both station inhabitants and visitors. The souk is alive with activity at almost all hours, with some establishments “on rotation” in terms of their open hours if they don’t have enough staff to stay open at all times. Beneath the inner surface of the drum, multiple decks make their way “down” and out towards the outer hull, where the bulk of the station’s accommodations, housing, officers, maintenance, and other facilities are located. These are the maze of corridors and rooms found on many ships and stations, although here they are somewhat more spacious. Broadly speaking, the “green” decks closer to the inner drum and the acres are a bit more secure and easier for station security to access, while the “black” decks closer to the outer hull are not patrolled quite as much, and don’t have as fast a response-time from station security.

The Docks

The docking ports on the station’s outer hull make Medina the crossroads of the galaxy, a place where ships transiting the zone can resupply, offload cargo and passengers, and generally take care of their needs without necessarily having to transit through another gate into a different system. The station has docking facilities for ten or so medium-sized ships, perhaps four capital-class ships, although they rarely dock other than for “shore leave” for their crews, shuttling people back and forth. There are numerous bays for shuttles and smaller craft. Medina’s facilities can also handle small repairs and regular maintenance, but the station is not a shipyard, as its repair crews regularly remind people. Traffic control through the gates and the Slow Zone is Medina Station’s primary task, one the Transport Union takes quite seriously. Just one ship entering or leaving out of order can potentially overload the gate network, causing one or more ships to disappear forever, and threatening other navigational hazards. While the slow zone may seem vast, ships traveling at high speeds can potentially collide or threaten other issues, so Medina traffic control expects all transiting vessels to follow protocols and wait their turn when it comes to arrivals, docking, and departures.

The Hub

At the center of the slow zone is a Builder artifact known commonly as “the hub” or “the ring station.” Its exterior is perfectly spherical and appears to be some form of burnished metallic blue that glows softly. The hub is approximately five kilometers in diameter, and its interior is known to contain various chambers and passages, but access is limited; James Holden found his way inside using his connection to the protomolecule with the assistance of a virtual version of Detective Josephus Miller. He was able to cause the station’s surface to iris open, but further attempts to do so have been unsuccessful. The interior parts of the hub contain insect-like mechanical constructs of the Builders, likely for maintenance and defense of its systems. Like most Builder technology, they remain dormant unless they detect a threat or otherwise need to take action. During his interaction with the hub, Holden perceived a vision of the Builders using it to sterilize entire star systems through the ring gates in an effort to fend off some type of threat. He was also able to “reset” the hub station’s system, lifting the speed limit on the Slow Zone and reopening the remaining 1373 gates in the zone. Ever since, the hub has been largely quiet and eerily inactive. During the Free Navy occupation of the Slow Zone and Medina Station, the hub station was equipped with six massive rail gun emplacements that had to be attached via metallic bands encircling the station since its surface resisted drilling or any other means of mounting. This gave the rail guns a full field of fire on the entire Slow Zone, including all of the gates. During the first Battle of Medina Station, coalition forces destroyed the rail gun emplacements while trying to seize control of them, but they have since been replaced. Initial forays into the Slow Zone, and later conflicts, resulted in a growing ring of debris in orbit around the hub station. Since the Transport Union took over, there has been an effort to clean up the area and remove any remaining debris, both to minimize navigational hazards and to reduce the chances of stray debris falling to the surface of the hub or otherwise “disturbing” it in any way. There are ongoing efforts to study the ring station, but they’re slowed by the inability to enter it or for scanning devices to penetrate its outer shell. The last thing anyone wants is to “alarm” the station’s systems, possibly leading to a repeat of what happened in the Slow Zone, or worse. In general, humanity gives the hub a wide berth and tries to leave it alone, focusing on the fact that the ring gates work rather than too much on how they work.

Spread out around the perimeter of the Slow Zone, each about half a million kilometers from the hub station, are the 1,373 rings, identical to the Sol Ring, that form gates to different star systems scattered across the galaxy. In the decades since those rings opened, humanity has been exploring, surveying, studying and—most particularly—settling and colonizing those systems. Once limited to a single system, humans are now scattered throughout the galaxy, although it remains to be seen if these tenuous beachheads beneath distant stars will last or be washed away by forces far larger and more powerful than anyone can imagine. Technically, the Earth-Mars Coalition issues charters for parties to survey, explore, and colonize different sites and worlds in the different systems, while the Transport Union manages traffic through the rings and the Slow Zone as well as the various systems, particularly Sol. Practice is a different matter, however. Not long after the gates first opened, there was a “ring rush” as people and ships from all over the system hurled themselves through the gates into the unknown. This led to many initial claims of rights to a particular discovery, ranging from a resource on a particular planet to the entire planet or even star system. Many, many such claims are caught up in legal action within the courts of the United Nations, and many of the litigants are powerful corporate interests, able to devote a substantial amount of time and resources to winning their cases. Individuals and smaller groups rarely have the ability to compete, and either have to try and fight it out, surrender, or find some settlement they can agree to.

The Survey Group

Following the conflict on Ilus, the International Astronomical Survey Group (IASG), in cooperation with the Earth-Mars Coalition, chartered a series of missions to do a comprehensive survey of all of the rings of the gate system. Initial surveys involved remote probes sent through the gates to determine what was on the other side followed by small survey missions meant to map the systems, discover if they had terrestrial planets, and investigate them further. One such mission—Comprehensive Ring Survey 673—was on the surface of such a planet when the breakaway Martian First Fleet transited into the system and claimed the planet as “Laconia.” They have not been heard from since. The Comprehensive Survey missions made wide-scale colonization more feasible and effective. Later in the Transport Union era, there are thriving settlements on many habitable worlds throughout the gate network, some of them with populations in the tens or even hundreds of millions. Although initially all colonial populations were immigrants, primarily from Earth and Mars, one of the first things stable settlements began doing was having children, and later in the era, there is a whole generation of humanity born and raised under other stars having never known the light of Sol.

Known Gate Systems

The following is just a handful of the known systems beyond the ring gates, what has been found there, and the various colonies and settlements established following the Free Navy Conflict.

Adro

A dead system with a white dwarf star, the only orbital body in the Adro system other than the ring is a massive sphere of translucent carbon-lattice diamond about the size of Jupiter. It is believed to be a builder artifact some five billion years old.

Arcadia

Arcadia III is a terrestrial world with heavier (1.5 g) gravity and a diverse biome full of hearty plants and often exoskel-etal or armored animals. The initial research colony has grown substantially under their “Humanity Coalition” government, having established a planetary constitution cherry-picking what the settlers consider the best parts of Earth and Martian laws.

Auberon

One of the most successful colony worlds, Auberon has a biome hospitable to earthly life, allowing crops and livestock to be raised there. Its capital and largest city is Barradan, but it has eleven other cities and tens of millions of inhabitants. Two particular oddities of Auberon are its short rotational period of eight hours, meaning a conventional twelve-hour day sees two sunrises and sunsets and “night” sees one of each. Additionally, its atmosphere smells “like a sewer” because of concentrations of the organic compound indole in its biome.

Bara Gaon

The Survey Series

The Comprehensive Survey Missions at the start of the Transport Union era make a great framework for an Expanse RPG series: The crew is part of a survey mission or, more likely, the crew of a ship transporting survey missions through different rings to explore them. In the latter case, they’re likely bringing survey mission personnel to mostly terrestrial worlds that have already been discovered by probes or earlier missions and dropping them off before going back through the ring to pick up their next assignment. Such surveyors can encounter any number of unknown challenges on diverse worlds, along with running into issues with habitable worlds that have “squatters” on them, unexpected trouble or technical issues, Laconian spies or agents infiltrating surveys, and more.

Ganymede agro-corp and a progressive Muslim community from the Greater Terai Interest Zone on Earth, the successful partnership has led to the colonization of three planets and two moons of a gas giant in the system. An independent mining operation currently has its eyes set on the system’s mineral-rich asteroid belt.

Castila

A damp, often cloudy forested world, Castila V has four continents and ancient “cultivated” structures made up of living trees the size of entire cities. A mix of Earther and Belter settlers have moved into these structures, modifying them for their own use.

Charon

A dead trinary star system. There is a planet in the Charon system where it rains shards of glass, as well as a vast crystalline “flower” construct in orbit around its star that appears to be a builder artifact of some sort.

Corazon Sagrado

With light (0.5 g) gravity and shallow, mineral-rich oceans that are often more like hot-springs, Corazon Sagrado has developed both a reputation as a kind of planetary spa for rest, relaxation, and recovery, and a world where Belters who want to live down a gravity well can easily settle far away from the conflicts between Earth and Mars. The mostly Belter population has created small communities following their own culture, although they welcome outsiders since tourism is a significant part of the colony’s economy.

Eudoxia

One of the first systems colonized by humans after the opening of the ring gates, Eudoxia has multiple settlements and a population in the tens of millions.

Firdaws

Two small, habitable planets in this system orbit each other, spinning around a stable axis point in their mutual orbit around the star rather than rotating on their own axes. This leaves some spots on both worlds in perpetual darkness. There must have been contact between the two worlds in the past, as life on both is highly genetically compatible, having diverged evolutionarily only in the (comparatively) recent past.

Freehold

Slightly smaller than Mars, the first planet in the Freehold system is terrestrial, albeit somewhat arid. True to their name, Freeholders are highly independent and libertarian, looking to avoid the heavy hand of the Earth-Mars Coalition and only barely observing the rules of the Transport Union thus far. Given that Freehold still needs to import biologicals and other necessary materials, that may lead to a problem if the colony continues to flout the Union’s rules.

Fusang

The dark world of Fusang is one of near-constant volcanic activity and highly alkaline, shallow seas. Even the plant life on Fusang is virtually black to absorb the limited light that reaches it, but the plants appear to scrub the atmosphere of ash and toxic gases, sequestering carbon in particular. Some of the plants have even developed limited mobility in the absence of any animal life. With the planet’s light 0.5 g, Fusang is home to Belter colonists and scientists studying its unique ecosystem.

Gedara

The habitable planet in the Gedara system has a high concentration of fissionable materials in its crust, leading to efforts to set up mining operations there.

Ilus

Ilus became famous as both the site of the first extrasolar conflict between colonists and corporate interests and also the first extrasolar disaster—an ancient builder fusion reactor on the planet reactivated and then exploded. The resulting shockwave and tsunami devastated much of the surface of Ilus. Were it not for rich deposits of lithium, the planet might have been abandoned, but colonists persevered; the colony on Ilus has grown considerably over the years.

Jannah

This system has a main-sequence star, two habitable planets, four gas giants, and a thin asteroid belt. Half a dozen different entities have put in claims to the two life-sustaining worlds, and planetary and ecological surveys have occasionally seen some conflict as one party or the other claims the absolute right to one or both planets. The innermost planet has some impressive, somewhat humanoid, megafauna.

Jerusalem

The Jerusalem system is one of the first gates where a ship went dutchman and disappeared.

Kronos

This system has no habitable planets, but there is sufficient lished for hundreds of rock hoppers. Kronos’s star, a red supergiant, has expanded and nearly consumed its original habitable world, shifting the habitable zone and allowing for liquid water and primitive algae to appear on one of the previously frozen moons of a gas giant in the outer system.

Laconia

The system named Laconia by Martian expatriates has a habitable planet in the second orbit from its star. There is also an ancient builder platform in orbit above the planet, likely the reason why Winston Duarte chose it for his breakaway colony. Laconia’s gate has been interdicted since the Free Navy Conflict, with the Laconians threatening to destroy anything that comes through it. In response, the Earth-Mars Coalition has parked at least one battleship outside the Laconia gate to keep watch on it should anything come through. Thus far, nothing has.

Longdune

A placid world of shallow seas with only numerous island chains for landmasses. The combination of 1 g, a 26-hour day, and a warm, stable climate has made Longdune a popular settlement site for Earthers. Gathered in small communities on the individual islands, each settlement usually has a

Room to Grow

The following systems are named in The Expanse source material, but no details are known about them. As Expanse Game Masters, feel free to develop them as you see fit!

Asylum, Athens, Farhome, Gethen, Gossner, Hakuseki, Hamshalim, Harris, Haza, Hope, Kalma, New Cyprus, New Kashmir, Pátria, Sigurtá, Tabalta, Walton, Xicheng, Yasamal

The known gates from The Expanse novels described here (including the Sol gate) plus the additional gates from the Beyond the Ring sourcebook from Green Ronin Publishing, and the remaining named gates from the novels listed here, are together not even one-twentieth of the total number of gates in the Slow Zone. There are well over a thousand still available for Expanse Game Masters to develop on their own, using the guidelines in the Beyond the Ring sourcebook—material for many years of Expanse RPG play during the Transport Union era, if you so desire.

Naraka

Although now a dead system, Naraka was once living so far as surveys can tell. It appears likely multiple planets in the system were terrestrial, but all five are now nothing more than shat - tered asteroid fields, their former satellites occupying their remaining orbits. Naraka is considered a useful system to hide out in, given the sheer number of orbital objects, and has been investigated for mining but not much else.

New Egypt

The fifth planet in its system, New Egypt is a desert world with no water to speak of, and yet life somehow manages to exist there. Its short rotational period gives it 18-hour days, and it has about a third of a g surface gravity. Martian terraforming techniques have adapted well to the dry and dusty planet, with ice-laden asteroids offering local sources of water for the New Egypt colony.

New Mars

The dusty yellow world of New Mars has appealed to Martians still interested in terraforming but wanting a “head start” on an arid world that has a breathable atmosphere and doesn’t require domes. They have already made a considerable leap forward by adding water to the planet and expanding its small oases, while also exploiting the mineral resources that apparently led the builders to place mining rigs in different spots on the surface.

Nieuwestad

Jacobin-Black Combined Capital, an industrial construction and climate engineering corporation, has a contract to conduct a comprehensive geological survey on the habitable planet in the system.

Paris

The most extensively builder-altered planet discovered yet discovered, Paris’s single continent is completely “paved” with an unknown alloy similar to the structure of the ring gates, with rows of structures of the same material. Many of these are intact and in use by the largely Martian colonists where they are accessible.

Persephone

The second planet in its system, Persephone is flanked on either side by asteroid fields in the neighboring orbits. Beyond lie the nine gas giants of its outer system. The planet’s surface is largely water, with small, rocky island chains and land masses, as well as extensive underwater caves. Persephone’s two moons and seven moonlets give it complex tides, although the planet is otherwise fairly placid. Colonists were a loose confederation of Belters and refugees from Ganymede that has grown over the years, now settling some of the larger landmasses.

San Estaban

One of the first settled systems surveyed by Royal Charter Energy, San Estaban’s habitable world is a moon of one of its gas giants. It has a population of eighteen million spread across ten cities. The colony was the first to map out the relative locations of the known ring systems throughout the galaxy using parallax matching of known stars.

Sanctuary

The largest moon of the smallest gas giant of the Sanctuary system is a habitable planetoid.

Tasnim

This system is one of the first gates where a ship went dutchman and disappeared while transiting.

Tecoma

This system has an unstable neutron star and no orbital objects whatsoever. Tecoma’s gate is in-line with the axis of the star, rather than its orbital plane.

Thanjavur

A colony of some 80,000 people is thriving on the habitable planet in the Thanjavur system.

Tridevi

This system has three habitable planets, named Saraswati, Laskhmi, and Parvati, all of which have thriving colonies and cities, totaling several million people.
